title: Why passing the product test does not prove readiness
summary: Understand why product knowledge alone does not establish readiness, and assess how learners apply it during realistic conversations and tasks.
body_markdown:
Knowing a process and performing it during a customer conversation are different demands. A training programme needs evidence of both, especially when people must listen, navigate tools and make decisions at the same time.


## Knowledge is necessary


A representative needs accurate product and policy knowledge. Tests can reveal gaps in that foundation and help trainers identify what to explain again. The problem is treating that result as evidence that the learner can already perform the complete job.


## Execution introduces different demands


On a real interaction, the customer may be unclear, frustrated or missing information. The representative has to find the right record, choose a permitted action and explain what happens next. An answer that sounds correct in a classroom may not translate into the right sequence of actions.


## Practise the complete task


Use a representative scenario that combines the conversation with the relevant tools. Make the success criteria explicit, including critical mistakes and escalation boundaries. Allow practice and feedback before asking the person to demonstrate readiness independently.


## Keep readiness contextual


Passing one scenario is not universal certification. Assess the responsibilities the person will actually take on and identify what still requires supervision. Use early live-work feedback to check whether the assessment was a useful predictor and adjust the programme when it was not.


## Connect training to the transition into work


Solidroad provides a way to practise and assess simulated tasks before a real customer is involved. The goal is a better-informed handoff from training into supported work, with evidence about what each person can do and where they still need help.
